nodes.label: Aristonicus and Asia
nodes.full: When Attalus III's kingdom passed to Rome, his half-brother Aristonicus claimed the throne, raised the poor, slaves and Greek cities and took the name Eumenes III. The war lasted four years, killed a Roman consul and ended with the capture of Aristonicus. The Senate then organised the province of Asia.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.1.38; Justin 36.4; Florus 1.35; Diodorus 34.2.

nodes.label: War on Aristonicus
nodes.full: Aristonicus defeated the consul P. Licinius Crassus Mucianus near Leucae in 130 BC, and Crassus was killed. M. Perperna crushed him the next year. The revolt, which promised the freed slaves the 'City of the Sun' (Heliopolis), was the last time the poor of Asia rose against Rome.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.1.38; Justin 36.4; Florus 1.35.

nodes.label: Tithe of Asia
nodes.full: Gaius Gracchus's law of 123 BC put up the tithe of Asia for auction at Rome, to be collected by companies of tax-farmers, the publicani. The system made fortunes for Roman equestrians and drained the provincials. Cicero called the tax-farmers of Asia the flower of the equestrian order.
nodes.src: Cicero, Verrines 3.12, Pro lege Manilia 15–17; Appian, Civil Wars 5.4; Peter Brunt, Roman Imperial Themes (1990).

nodes.label: Cicero’s letter
nodes.full: Cicero wrote to his brother Quintus, governor of Asia for three years, a long letter of advice: restrain your staff, listen to the Greeks, remember that Asia is a province of cities with their own pride, and avoid the extortions that the tax-farmers' friends will urge. It is the Republic's best statement of provincial ethics.
nodes.src: Cicero, Ad Quintum fratrem 1.1.

nodes.label: Richest province
nodes.full: Cicero told the Roman people that Asia was so rich and fertile that in the fruitfulness of its soil, the variety of its crops and the extent of its pastures and the volume of its exports it outdid all other lands. The province's tithes and customs duties paid a large part of Rome's expenses.
nodes.src: Cicero, Pro lege Manilia 14; Strabo 12–14; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 61.

nodes.label: Mithridates VI
nodes.full: Mithridates VI of Pontus, a Greek-educated king of Persian descent who claimed to be Alexander's heir, conquered the Black Sea coast, pushed into Bithynia, Cappadocia and Asia, massacred the Romans of Asia in 88 and fought Rome in three wars before he was forced to suicide. He is the Republic's most dangerous eastern enemy.
nodes.src: Appian, Mithridatic Wars; Plutarch, Sulla, Lucullus, Pompey; Justin 37–38; Adrienne Mayor, The Poison King (2010).

nodes.label: Asiatic Vespers
nodes.full: Mithridates VI ordered the killing of all Romans and Italians in Asia on a single day. Ancient sources say 80,000 (Plutarch 150,000) were killed, many seized from the altars of temples. The massacre bound the Greek cities of Asia to Mithridates and brought Sulla's army to the East.
nodes.src: Appian, Mithridatic Wars 22–23; Valerius Maximus 9.2; Plutarch, Sulla 24.

nodes.label: Sulla and Dardanus
nodes.full: Sulla beat Mithridates's armies in Greece at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, crossed to Asia and in 85 made the peace of Dardanus: Mithridates returned to Pontus, gave up his conquests and paid 2,000 talents. Sulla then punished the cities that had rebelled and imposed an indemnity of 20,000 talents and the quartering of his army.
nodes.src: Appian, Mithridatic Wars 54–64; Plutarch, Sulla 22–25.

nodes.label: Lucullus and Pompey
nodes.full: In the Third Mithridatic War Lucullus broke the siege of Cyzicus in 73–72 by starving Mithridates's army, and drove him into Armenia. Pompey took command in 66 and beat Mithridates by night near Nicopolis. Mithridates fled to the Crimea and, in 63, had himself killed by a soldier at Panticapaeum.
nodes.src: Appian, Mithridatic Wars 72–113; Plutarch, Lucullus 9–36, Pompey 31–42.

nodes.label: Pompey and the pirates
nodes.full: Cilician pirate fleets had captured Roman magistrates, raided Italian ports and stopped the grain supply. Pompey was given a command over the whole Mediterranean by the lex Gabinia and in three months cleared the sea. He settled the pirates in inland and coastal cities, notably at Soli, which was renamed Pompeiopolis.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Pompey 24–28; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 91–96; Cassius Dio 36.20–37.

nodes.label: Pompey’s settlement
nodes.full: Pompey, after his victories over Mithridates and the pirates, organised the eastern lands into provinces and client states: Bithynia and Pontus as one province, Cilicia enlarged, and kings in Galatia, Cappadocia and Paphlagonia. He founded cities and thirty-nine colonies. The system was the framework of Roman Anatolia for a century.
nodes.src: Strabo 12.3.1; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 114–115; Plutarch, Pompey 38–45.

nodes.label: Deiotarus, Amyntas
nodes.full: Deiotarus, tetrarch of the Tolistobogii, became king of Galatia and Lesser Armenia, an ally of Pompey, then of Caesar and of Cicero's defence, and raised legions on the Roman model. His successor Amyntas, who built up a kingdom in Pisidia, died in 25 BC, and Augustus made Galatia a Roman province.
nodes.src: Cicero, Pro rege Deiotaro; Strabo 12.5.1, 12.6.1; Stephen Mitchell, Anatolia (1993).

nodes.label: Nemrud Dağ
nodes.full: Antiochus I of Commagene built on a mountain summit a funerary mound and cult terraces with colossal seated statues of himself and of syncretic gods — Zeus-Oromasdes, Apollo-Mithras-Helios-Hermes, Artagnes-Heracles-Ares — whose names combine Persian and Greek. A long Greek inscription lays down the cult. It is a monument to a small kingdom's claim to be heir to both Persians and Macedonians.
nodes.src: Nemrud Dağ hierothesion inscription (Orientis Graeci Inscriptiones Selectae 383); Donald Sanders, Nemrud Dağ (1996); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 448.

nodes.label: Strabo
nodes.full: Strabo, born at Amasia in Pontus to a family of Mithridates's courtiers, wrote a Geography of the Roman world in 17 books, drawing on the earlier geographers and his own travels. His account of Anatolia, in books 12 to 14, is the standard description of the peninsula in the Augustan age.
nodes.src: Strabo, Geography 12–14.

nodes.label: Brutus and Cassius
nodes.full: After Caesar's murder, Brutus and Cassius took money and ships from the cities of Asia for the war against Antony and Octavian. Brutus besieged Xanthos in Lycia, whose people killed themselves rather than surrender as they had against the Persians, and Cassius sacked Rhodes. Antony's tribute demands followed.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Brutus 30–32; Appian, Civil Wars 4.73–82.

nodes.label: Parthian invasion
nodes.full: Quintus Labienus, a Roman Republican officer who had joined the Parthians, and the prince Pacorus invaded Syria and Anatolia in 40 BC and held much of Cilicia and Asia for a year. Ventidius drove them out in a series of battles. It was the first Parthian incursion into Anatolia.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 48.24–41; Plutarch, Antony 33.

nodes.label: Aphrodisias archive wall
nodes.full: The city of Aphrodisias, favoured by Octavian and Sulla, had the letters from emperors and decrees of the Senate granting it freedom and tax immunity inscribed on a wall of its theatre, the Archive Wall. The surviving documents show a city using its history to win privilege.
nodes.src: Joyce Reynolds, Aphrodisias and Rome (1982); Aphrodisias excavation (Kenan Erim, 1961–90).

nodes.label: Sebasteion
nodes.full: Two parallel porticoes of three storeys led to a temple of the Julio-Claudian emperors and Aphrodite, with scores of relief panels of mythology, personified nations and emperors in heroic nudity. They were made by local sculptors from the Aphrodisias marble quarries. It is the most complete picture of imperial ideology in a provincial city.
nodes.src: R. R. R. Smith, 'The Imperial Reliefs from the Sebasteion at Aphrodisias', Journal of Roman Studies 77 (1987); Smith, The Marble Reliefs from the Julio-Claudian Sebasteion (2013).

nodes.label: Augustus and Asia
nodes.full: Augustus allowed the provincials of Asia to build temples to Rome and himself at Pergamon in 29 BC (the first such cult for a living ruler), reformed the tax system, made Galatia a province in 25 BC and gave his support to the rebuilding of the earthquake-damaged cities. He had been the patron of Asia for a generation, and Asia made him a god.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 51.20; Res Gestae Divi Augusti; Suetonius, Augustus 47–48.

nodes.label: Veteran colonies
nodes.full: Augustus founded colonies of discharged veterans at Antioch in Pisidia, Lystra, Parlais, Cremna, Olbasa and Comama in the 20s BC to hold the Taurus and to Romanise the region. They were islands of Latin in a Greek and native sea, which Paul visited.
nodes.src: Strabo 12.6.4; Res Gestae 28; Barbara Levick, Roman Colonies in Southern Asia Minor (1967).

nodes.label: Homanades war
nodes.full: The Homanades, mountain tribes of the central Taurus who had raided the plains and the Pisidian colonies, were fought by Quirinius, governor of Galatia, in a long campaign of blockade and starvation that left the region quiet until the later empire. It was Rome's work to secure Galatia and its colonies.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 3.48; Strabo 12.6.5; Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Via Sebaste
nodes.full: Augustus's governor of Galatia, Cornutus Aquila, built a road linking the Pisidian colonies from Antioch to Lystra and Iconium, with milestones of Latin text and veterans settled along it. It was the military road by which Rome held the Taurus, and the one on which Paul and Barnabas travelled.
nodes.src: Milestones of the Via Sebaste (Inscriptions of Pisidian Antioch); Stephen Mitchell and Marc Waelkens, Pisidian Antioch (1998).

nodes.label: Calendar of Asia
nodes.full: The Council of Asia decided in 9 BC, on a proposal of the proconsul Paullus Fabius Maximus, to begin the civil year on Augustus's birthday, 23 September, since 'the birthday of the god was for the world the beginning of good news'. The inscription, found at Priene and elsewhere, shows the language of the imperial cult at work, and is often cited for the background to the Gospel.
nodes.src: Priene calendar inscription (Orientis Graeci Inscriptiones Selectae 458); Simon Price, Rituals and Power (1984).

nodes.label: Res Gestae at Ancyra
nodes.full: Augustus's testament, listing his deeds, expenses and honours, was carved in Latin and Greek on the walls of the temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra, with parallel copies at Apollonia and Antioch in Pisidia. It is the best surviving statement of the Augustan regime in its own words.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Augusti (Monumentum Ancyranum), ed. Alison Cooley (2009).

nodes.label: Cappadocia annexed
nodes.full: When King Archelaus of Cappadocia was called to Rome and died in 17 AD, Tiberius made his kingdom a province, with a procurator at Caesarea; its revenues allowed him to halve the sales tax. Claudius reorganised Lycia as a province in 43 and put an end to its league's liberties. Nero's Armenian wars used Cappadocia as a base.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 2.42, 2.56, 12.55; Suetonius, Claudius 25; Cassius Dio 60.17.

nodes.label: Earthquake of 17
nodes.full: In a single night in 17 AD an earthquake destroyed twelve cities of western Asia, Sardis worst of all. Tiberius gave ten million sesterces to Sardis and remitted the taxes of all the stricken cities for five years. The cities set up statues and temples in thanks, and Sardis was the greatest beneficiary.
nodes.src: Tacitus, Annals 2.47; Pliny, Natural History 2.200; Strabo 12.8.18.

nodes.label: Paul at Ephesus
nodes.full: Paul spent about two years at Ephesus, and the book of Acts tells of how his preaching reduced the trade in silver shrines of Artemis and caused a riot in the theatre, with a crowd chanting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians'. The city's Christian community, by the second century, was among the largest of Asia.
nodes.src: Acts 19:1–41; Paul's Corinthian letters; Clinton Arnold, Ephesians: Power and Magic (1989).

nodes.label: Corbulo
nodes.full: Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, appointed to Cappadocia and Galatia by Nero, trained the soft eastern legions with a winter's discipline and took Armenia's capitals from Parthia. He was then made to accept a settlement in which the Armenian king took his crown from the Roman emperor. Corbulo was ordered to commit suicide in 67.

nodes.label: Vespasian’s East
nodes.full: Vespasian annexed Commagene and Lesser Armenia in 72 AD and joined Cappadocia and Galatia in one great military province with two legions on the upper Euphrates, to meet Parthian pressure. The old client kingdoms disappeared and the frontier became a line of forts, roads and garrisons.
nodes.src: Josephus, Jewish War 7.219–243; Suetonius, Vespasian 8; Barbara Levick on Anatolian military roads.

nodes.label: Zeugma
nodes.full: The 'bridge' city of Zeugma crossed the Euphrates at the frontier of Rome and Parthia, with a legionary base, a toll station and a trade in silks and spices. Its rich houses were decorated with mosaics, which came to light before the flooding of the Birecik dam in 2000. The Sasanians sacked it in 256.
nodes.src: Zeugma excavations (Kenan Erim, Roger Early); Gaziantep Zeugma Mosaic Museum; Pliny, Natural History 5.86.

nodes.label: Dioscorides
nodes.full: Dioscorides, an army doctor from Cilicia, wrote De Materia Medica, five books on about six hundred plants and a thousand drugs, with descriptions of their sources, preparation and effects. It became the main pharmacology of the West and the East for fifteen centuries.
nodes.src: Dioscorides, De Materia Medica; Vienna Dioscorides manuscript (c. 512).

nodes.label: Seven churches
nodes.full: The Revelation of John is addressed to seven Christian communities of western Anatolia — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamon, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea — with a message to each. It shows a well-developed Christian network, and its tension with the imperial cult.
nodes.src: Revelation 1–3; Colin Hemer, The Letters to the Seven Churches of Asia (1986).

nodes.label: Trajan to Antonines
nodes.full: Under Trajan, Hadrian and the Antonines the cities of Asia saw their greatest prosperity: they were visited by Hadrian in 123–124 and 129, graced with temples and new monuments, and given the status of neokoroi of the imperial cult. They competed for rank and titles.
nodes.src: Historia Augusta, Hadrian; Cassius Dio 69; Aelius Aristides, Orations 17, 21–23; Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Pliny and Trajan
nodes.full: Pliny the Younger, sent as special legate to Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor on every detail: a fire brigade for Nicomedia, accounts of city finances, aqueducts and canals, and what to do with Christians. Trajan's replies give the empire's rule for provincial government.
nodes.src: Pliny, Epistulae 10.15–121, esp. 10.33–34 (fire brigade), 10.96–97 (Christians).

nodes.label: Polycarp
nodes.full: The aged bishop Polycarp was arrested and brought before the proconsul in the stadium of Smyrna, asked to swear by the emperor's fortune and curse Christ, and replied that he had served him for eighty-six years. He was burned. The letter on his martyrdom is the earliest account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament.
nodes.src: Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. 155–160); Eusebius, Church History 4.15.

nodes.label: Montanus
nodes.full: Around 157 AD Montanus, a Phrygian, began to prophesy in a trance, with two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, that the Holy Spirit was speaking in them and that the heavenly Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza. The movement, which spread to North Africa and won over Tertullian, was condemned by the Asian synods.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Church History 5.16–19; Epiphanius, Panarion 48; Christine Trevett, Montanism (1996).

nodes.label: Confession steles
nodes.full: Peasants of the upper Hermus valley set up small stone steles confessing sins — perjury, adultery, using a sacred spring or the property of a god — for which the god had punished them with illness or death, and which they now made public in atonement. They show a world of rural Anatolian religion that had little to do with the cities.
nodes.src: Georg Petzl, Die Beichtinschriften Westkleinasiens (1994).

nodes.label: Library of Celsus
nodes.full: Julius Aquila built at Ephesus a library in memory of his father, Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, consul in 92 and governor of Asia, with a two-storey facade of columns and niches with statues of the Virtues, and with his tomb in the crypt. It held about twelve thousand scrolls and is one of the best-preserved Roman monuments in Anatolia.
nodes.src: Inscription of the library of Celsus (Inschriften von Ephesos 5101); Wilhelm Wilberg and Austrian excavations, Forschungen in Ephesos.

nodes.label: Aspendos
nodes.full: A Roman theatre built under Marcus Aurelius by the architect Zenon, son of Theodorus, with a scaenae frons still standing and seating for about twelve thousand. It is the best-preserved Roman theatre in the Mediterranean and is still used for performance.
nodes.src: Inscriptions of the theatre of Aspendos (Zenon of Aspendos); Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Hadrian’s journeys
nodes.full: Hadrian toured the provinces of Asia in 123–124 and again in 129, restoring the temples of Cyzicus and Ephesus, founding the new cities of Hadrianoutherae and Hadrianopolis and establishing the Panhellenion of Greek cities. The emperor himself was a Greek enthusiast, the 'Graeculus'.
nodes.src: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 13; Cassius Dio 69.10–12; Anthony Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor (1997).

nodes.label: Antinous
nodes.full: Antinous, a youth from Bithynion in Bithynia, became the companion of the emperor Hadrian and drowned in the Nile in 130. Hadrian had him deified, founded the city of Antinoopolis and set up a cult across the empire, with his image on coins of Anatolian cities. The relation between a mature man and a youth was recognised in Greek and Roman custom; the sources do not say how Antinous himself saw it.
nodes.src: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 14; Cassius Dio 69.11; Caroline Vout, Power and Eroticism in Imperial Rome (2007).

nodes.label: Plancia Magna
nodes.full: Plancia Magna, daughter of a governor of Bithynia and wife of an Anatolian senator, held the city offices of demiourgos and of priestess of Artemis Pergaia in Perge, and paid for the monumental city gate with its niches for statues of her family and the founders of the city. Her statue base survives.
nodes.src: Perge inscriptions (Plancia Magna, Inschriften von Perge); Mary Boatwright, Hadrian and the Cities of the Roman Empire (2000).

nodes.label: Golden age of cities
nodes.full: Under the Pax Romana the cities of Anatolia grew rich and built on a vast scale — theatres, gymnasia, baths, aqueducts, libraries — with their elites competing for titles and temples in the empire's name. Hundreds of cities stood in the peninsula by the second century. It is the age that gave Ephesus, Pergamon, Sardis, Aphrodisias and Perge their ruins.
nodes.src: A. H. M. Jones, The Cities of the Eastern Roman Provinces (1937); Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Ephesus emporium
nodes.full: Ephesus was the capital of Asia and by Strabo's account the greatest emporium of the province west of the Taurus, with a population estimated at a quarter of a million. It was the seat of the proconsul, the temple warden, the gymnasia and the largest Greek market for the trade between Italy and the East.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.1.24; Pausanias 7.2; Peter Scherrer (ed.), Ephesus: The New Guide (2000).

nodes.label: Ephesus harbour
nodes.full: The Cayster river silted up the harbour of Ephesus, and its engineers dredged and rebuilt it in turn under Attalus II, Nero and Hadrian, with a canal and a new harbour gate. Strabo said that the king's dredging only worsened the silting. By late antiquity the sea was out of reach.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.1.24; Helmut Brückner on the Ephesus harbour (geoarchaeology).

nodes.label: Imperial marble
nodes.full: The Romans took over the quarries of white and coloured marble in Phrygia (Docimium, 'pavonazzetto') and on the Marmara island of Proconnesus, which became imperial properties. Their stone was exported to build and decorate the monuments of Rome and the provinces and made sarcophagi for the whole eastern Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Strabo 12.8.14; Pliny, Natural History 36.46; Norman Herz and Marc Waelkens, Classical Marble (1988).

nodes.label: Hierapolis saw
nodes.full: A relief on a sarcophagus of the early third century at Hierapolis shows a water-powered stone-saw, with a wheel, gears and a connecting rod and crank turning rotary motion into reciprocal motion. It is the earliest known evidence for the crank and connecting rod, a basic machine element of later industry.
nodes.src: Hierapolis sarcophagus of Marcus Aurelius Ammianos; Tullia Ritti, Klaus Grewe and Paul Kessener, Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007).

nodes.label: Opramoas
nodes.full: Opramoas of Rhodiapolis, a rich Lycian notable, gave gifts to the cities of the Lycian League for some twenty-seven years — buildings, games, gifts of money and grain — to a total of some half a million denarii, recorded on the walls of his mausoleum. He is the best-documented of the civic benefactors, the euergetai, on whom the cities depended.
nodes.src: Opramoas inscription at Rhodiapolis (TAM II 905); Jean-Jacques Aubert, Business Managers (1994); Rouanet, Lycian studies.

nodes.label: Synagogue of Sardis
nodes.full: In the third century the Jewish community of Sardis took over and rebuilt a great hall in the city's bath-gymnasium complex as a synagogue, one of the largest of the ancient world, with a forecourt, mosaic floors and some eighty Greek donor inscriptions. It shows a community with a high civic standing and a long history, from the time of the Seleucids.
nodes.src: George Hanfmann and Andrew Seager, Sardis excavation reports; Josephus, Antiquities 14.235, 16.171.

nodes.label: Galen
nodes.full: Galen, born in Pergamon, trained at its Asklepieion, served as surgeon to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia, moved to Rome and became physician to emperors. He wrote hundreds of treatises on anatomy and medicine and dominated medicine until the Renaissance.
nodes.src: Galen, De methodo medendi; De libris propriis; Vivian Nutton, Ancient Medicine (2004).

nodes.label: Gladiators of Ephesus
nodes.full: In 1993 Austrian archaeologists found a cemetery at Ephesus with the bones of about seventy men, mostly aged 20 to 30, with injuries from weapons and a tomb relief of gladiators. The men were fighters of the games held in honour of the emperor. The gladiators of Asia were treated by doctors like Galen of Pergamon, who held the post for the high priest.
nodes.src: Karl Grossschmidt and Fabian Kanz, 'Die Gladiatoren von Ephesos', Journal of Roman Archaeology; Galen, De methodo medendi 4.

nodes.label: Aristides’s illness
nodes.full: Aelius Aristides, the famed orator, was ill for seventeen years and spent two years in the sanctuary of Asclepius at Pergamon, where the god sent him dreams, which he recorded in his Sacred Tales. The text gives, in a rich first person, the experience of illness, a healing cult and a patient's relation to a god.
nodes.src: Aelius Aristides, Hieroi Logoi (Sacred Tales); Brooke Holmes on ancient illness narratives.

nodes.label: Antonine plague
nodes.full: The plague that Roman soldiers brought back from Mesopotamia in 165–166 spread through the empire for fifteen years. Galen, in Rome, described it; Aelius Aristides was sick with it in Smyrna. Its death toll, which has been put at several million, is debated, but it hit the cities of Anatolia hard.
nodes.src: Galen, De methodo medendi 5.12; Cassius Dio 72.14; Aelius Aristides, Hieroi Logoi 2; Christer Bruun on the plague.

nodes.label: Arrian
nodes.full: Arrian, a Greek of Nicomedia, pupil of Epictetus, governor of Cappadocia in 131–137, wrote the Anabasis of Alexander, a history based on the lost accounts of Ptolemy and Aristobulus. As governor he repelled the Alans and wrote a handbook for the defence of the frontier.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis; Ektaxis kata Alanon; Periplus of the Euxine.

nodes.label: Thecla
nodes.full: The Acts of Paul and Thecla, a second-century narrative, tells of Thecla, a young woman of Iconium who left her fiancé to follow Paul's teaching on virginity, survived being thrown to beasts and baptised herself, and became a teacher. Her cult at Seleucia on the Calycadnus was very popular. The text is a story, but it shows what Christian women found in the faith.
nodes.src: Acts of Paul and Thecla; Stephen Davis, The Cult of Saint Thecla (2001).

nodes.label: Dio and Aristides
nodes.full: Dio Chrysostom of Prusa, an orator of the Flavian and Trajanic age, and Aelius Aristides of Smyrna, whose Roman Oration praised the empire in 143, were the leading figures of the Second Sophistic. They spoke on the cities' rivalry and the empire's blessings, in a Greek that harked back to classical Athens.
nodes.src: Dio Chrysostom, Orations 31–50; Aelius Aristides, Orations 26 (To Rome).

nodes.label: Septimius Severus
nodes.full: After defeating Pescennius Niger at Issus in 194, Severus punished the cities that had backed him, notably Nicaea and Byzantium, and favoured those that had backed him, such as Nicomedia. The Severan court, with its wars in the East, passed repeatedly through Anatolia, and Caracalla's citizenship edict was issued in 212.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 74–75; Herodian 3.1–6; Historia Augusta, Severus.

nodes.label: Cyzicus and Issus
nodes.full: Pescennius Niger, proclaimed emperor at Antioch, held Byzantium and most of Anatolia against Septimius Severus. Severus's armies won at Cyzicus and Nicaea in 193 and Issus in 194, where Niger was beaten, and the siege of Byzantium ended with its destruction in 196.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 74.6–75.14; Herodian 3.1–6.

nodes.label: Constitutio Antoniniana
nodes.full: Caracalla gave Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire, including the cities of Anatolia, where only a minority of city-dwellers had held it. A fragment survives on a papyrus from Egypt; its reasons — taxes or religion — are debated. After it, thousands of Anatolians were named Aurelius.
nodes.src: Papyrus Giessen 40; Cassius Dio 78.9; Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East (1993).

nodes.label: Cassius Dio
nodes.full: Cassius Dio, a senator from Nicaea in Bithynia, consul twice, wrote a Roman History in eighty books from Aeneas to his own day. His account of Augustus, Septimius Severus and the Severan court is a major source for the Principate by an eyewitness.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio, Roman History; Fergus Millar, A Study of Cassius Dio (1964).

nodes.label: Third-century crisis
nodes.full: The invasions, civil wars and debasement of the third century hit the cities of Anatolia hard: the building programmes stopped, the elites withdrew, city walls were thrown up and the number of inscriptions dropped. Recovery came with Diocletian and in Constantine's new empire.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.26–50; Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Shapur and the Goths
nodes.full: In the mid-third century Sasanian armies under Shapur I took Antioch and, in 260, the Roman emperor Valerian himself, then looted Cappadocia and Cilicia. Gothic raiders came by sea over several summers, and in 262 burned Ephesus and the Artemision. Cities built walls from their own temples and theatres.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Saporis; Zosimus 1.27–44; Historia Augusta, Gallieni 6.

nodes.label: Persian and Gothic invasions
nodes.full: Shapur I's armies raided Cappadocia, Cilicia and Lycaonia in the 250s, took Valerian prisoner in 260, and Gothic fleets sailed from the Black Sea to sack Ephesus and burn the Artemision in 262. The Palmyrene queen Zenobia held Anatolia as far as Ancyra before Aurelian beat her in 272.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Saporis; Zosimus 1.26–50; Historia Augusta, Gallieni and Aureliani; Mitchell 1993.

nodes.label: Christian Phrygia
nodes.full: In the villages of upper Phrygia, by the later third century, inscriptions on tombs were being set up 'by Christians for Christians', in a public statement that is rare for the empire. Eumeneia and Otrous had Christian majorities when Constantine became emperor.
nodes.src: Epitaphs of the Christians of Phrygia (MAMA vol. 7; Elsner and Mitchell, Anatolian Studies).

nodes.label: Diocletian
nodes.full: Diocletian, proclaimed at Nicomedia, made it his eastern capital from 286, with a palace, a circus, an arms factory and a mint. His reforms of provinces, army and taxes, and his Edict of Maximum Prices, were issued from there. He abdicated at Nicomedia in 305.
nodes.src: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 7–19; Aurelius Victor 39; Stephen Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985).

nodes.label: Edict of Prices
nodes.full: Diocletian issued a list of the maximum prices for over a thousand goods and wages across the empire, inscribed on stone in cities across Anatolia, including a long copy at Aphrodisias found in the 1970s. It tried to hold down inflation by decree and failed. It is the best source for prices in the late third century.
nodes.src: Edictum Diocletiani de pretiis, ed. Marta Giacchero (1974); Kenan Erim and Joyce Reynolds, Journal of Roman Studies 63 (1973).

nodes.label: Great Persecution
nodes.full: In February 303 the praetorian guard demolished the church of Nicomedia, within sight of Diocletian's palace, and the first edict was posted ordering churches destroyed, scriptures burned and Christians deprived of rights. A fire in the palace led to the arrests. The persecution lasted, in the East, for a decade.
nodes.src: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 12–15; Eusebius, Church History 8.2.

nodes.label: Constantine
nodes.full: Licinius ruled the East from Nicomedia after 313; the war with Constantine ended at Chrysopolis in 324. Constantine, now sole emperor, gathered the bishops at Nicaea in 325 and in 330 dedicated the new city of Constantinople on Byzantium's site on the Bosphorus, taking the centre of gravity of the empire to Anatolia's threshold.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Life of Constantine; Zosimus 2.18–30; Timothy Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981).

nodes.label: Council of Nicaea
nodes.full: Constantine summoned the bishops to Nicaea, the first ecumenical council, to settle the dispute over Arius's teaching that the Son was created. The council adopted the creed that the Son is of one substance with the Father, set a common date for Easter and gave some three hundred bishops their first imperial banquet.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.6–14; Athanasius, De decretis; Council of Nicaea canons.

nodes.label: Attalus III’s bequest
nodes.full: Attalus III of Pergamon died in 133 BC and left his kingdom to the Roman people in his will.
